title.narrative: Renewable Energy For Refugees, Phase II (RE4R Phase II)

description.narrative: Insatsen har som målsättning att öka tillgången och användingen av energi för utsatta människor i och utanför Rwandas fem flyktingläger. Med en marknadsansats kommer Practical Action öka tillgången till rena matlagningsmetoder, gatubelysning och förnybara ellösningar för hemmen. Under insatsen kommer också mindre företag få företagsutbildning och delfinansiering för energilösningar kopplade till deras företagsideer. Företagen kommer också ha tillgång till nya eller omgjorda företagscenter inom och utanför flyktinglägret. Insatsen har ett uttalat och välutvecklat jämställdhets fokus. Förändringar i matlagningsmetoder har i Rwanda en nära koppling till anpassningsåtgärder då avskogning i det bergiga landskapet är ett stort problem och leder till erosion.

The contribution aims to increase access to energy in Rwanda´s five refugee camps and their host communities. Practical action will use a market-based approach to increase access to clean cooking solutions, streetlights and renewable energy solutions in the homes. Small business will be supported with coaching and subsidies for their energy linked investments that are key to support their business models. Business will also have increased access to business centres in and outside of the camps. The contribution has a developed gender focus. In Rwanda, changing cooking methods are closely linked to efforts to avoid deforestation which in turn is an important adaptation measure as deforestation in combination with increased rainfalls leads to challenging erosion in the very hilly country.

The project is set to impact Rwanda's commitments to the Global Refugee Compact for Energy and Infrastructure and support achievement of SDG 7 for last mile communities. And the following outcomes and targets will support the achievement:
Outcome 1. Refugee communities in all camps in Rwanda and the surrounding host communities have access to affordable, low-carbon and environmentally friendly energy for household, business and community uses. By the end of the project there should be a 70% camp-wide uptake of minimum tier 1 renewable energy solutions for electricity. With regards to electricity for SME's, 300 enterprises should be reached through the Productive use of Energy (PUE) for livelihoods program. Furthermore, 80% of the total area of refugee camps is to be covered by public lighting and a number of renewable energy solution for institutions/community buildings in and around camps.
Outcome 2. Refugees in all camps and the surrounding host communities benefit from improved quality of life and livelihoods through strengthened markets and increased economic activity. 70% of households of target population self-report improved quality of life as a result of the project and 70% of supported PUE business report a 50% increase to their business income. Also, a total of 200 dignified jobs to be secured in refugee and host communities.
Outcome 3. Humanitarian stakeholders in Rwanda and in the wider, global humanitarian sector priorities renewable energy solutions, endorse, adopt and replicate Practical Action´s approach, and include refugee energy and livelihoods needs in their plans and policies at local, national and international levels 10 target stakeholders report they have planned or committed to adopt approaches promoted through the project 5 strategic practices at local, national, and international (including policies, response plans and project designs) have been informed or adapted to improve energy access for refugees and host communities as a result of the project.

sector.narrative: Energy generation, renewable sources - multiple technologies

description.narrative:
The project is implemented by the British INGO Practical Action (PA) with a local office in Kigali, fully staffed with local experts and a designated project manager. In March 2024 the project closed its first 20 months and it is implemented largely against the plan, but delivery of Solar Home systems and stoves are delayed. Below are summarised insights and results from the status update report (February 2024), the second narrative report (April 2024) and the Advisory Committee held in Karongi, 11 September, 2024.
Clean cooking- planned target: 9 400 cook stoves and fuels Practical Action has successfully formed contracts with three private partners: Ecogreen, MC Green, and Agroplast. These partners are responsible for distributing cook stoves and pellets within the camp and the host community across all five refugee camps. As of now, the companies have collectively sold 2,649 stoves and 294,800 kilograms of pellets. Ecogreen has sold 1,059 stoves and 146,060 kilograms of pellets, MC Green has sold 1,579 stoves and 148,740 kilograms of pellets, while Agroplast has sold a total of 11 stoves. The results are clearly below the targeted 9 400 cook stoves that was planned. Companies are facing challenges regarding the pricing that was negotiated with Practical Action generally due to foreign exchange rate and inflation in Rwanda during the past two years. There are also challenges related between the so called forced and natural air draft versions of the stoves where refugees naturally prefer the forced air draft stoves as they are more fuel efficient and also include a small solar device that also can be used for instance to charge a mobile. However, companies production capacities are challenged to meet the demand of forced air draft stoves.
Solar home systems (SHS)- planned target: 7 047 Solar Home systems Practical Action has effectively secured contracts with two private partners, Solektra and Belecom. Each company has implemented Solar Home Systems (SHS) throughout the five refugee camps. As of now, 1,980 SHS units have been sold and installed, with Solektra accounting for 780 installations and Belecom for 1,200 installations. Companies have suffered from increased foreign exchange rates and high inflation in the country. One company have met their annual targets, and the other have had unforeseen challenges in their supply chain. Practical Actions Community Mobilization and Inclusion Officers conducted physical verification and the feedback from beneficiaries of the Solar Hope System (SHS) has been positive. They express satisfaction with the system's quality compared to alternatives they used to purchase. The SHS light facilitates refugees to perform evening activities such as cooking, household chores, and business operations, providing illumination even during late hours. Additionally, it proves invaluable for students, enabling them to revise their studies at night, and simplifies access to latrines with the assistance of the provided torch. The SHS connections are made to a small majority of female led households (56%) Institutional/Solar streetlights, planned target: 815 street lights installed
Practical Action has signed a contract with Solektra Rwanda Limited for the supply and installation of solar streetlights across five refugee camps. The installation of 815 solar streetlights is complete and has greatly improved community life, facilitating social interactions, leisure activities, and mobility. Business centers and business supported- targets reached
To efficiently utilize energy, 300 entrepreneurs have been recruited and are receiving support. The construction of business centers in Kiziba and Mugombwa is completed. The business centre in Mugombwa hosts 50 entrepreneurs and Kiziba 40 entrepreneurs. In Kiziba 20 have already made their 30% equity contribution and received their appliances in July 2024. The Mahama business center's construction is well in progress and will be completed in November 2024. Practical Action has employed business mentors to provide continuous mentorship to all the entrepreneurs, focusing on business management and aiding them in securing equity for appliance acquisition.
For instance, March 2024, seven refugee women formed the Women Dairy Group (WDG). Under RE4R II, the group was supported with business mentorship training and access to financial capital. From this support, the group was able to procure a milk cooler and a freezer. Since June 2024, the groups income has increased from US$500 to $860. This additional finance has been used to support the women's families future, allowing them to invest in their childrens education. The WDG is playing a key role in strengthening the local market in Kiziba refugee camp. It has established a stable solution for local farmers to sell their milk for a set price of RWF 400 per liter. This is almost the double what some farmers previously received. The price attracts farmers from communities further away, expanding market reach and securing market linkages across the refugee and host communities. The WDG sells to local canteens, ensuring a consistent fresh supply of milk to local restaurants and food outlets. Recently, the group opened a canteen within Kiziba Refugee Camp, selling both fresh and fermented milk across the community. The owners of the WDG have become role models, demonstrating what is possible and inspiring peers to make their entrepreneurial ideas a reality.
Parallel with the above installations and business support: The creation of Gender Working Groups in five refugee camps, consisting of a total 41 women and 34 men, aims to foster dialogue and collaboration towards gender equity and inclusion. This initiative also enables both women and men to engage with renewable energy solutions, bolstering confidence and enhancing awareness about gender transformation and inclusion in the energy sector.
Under the productive use of energy (PUE) intervention, through peer-to-peer leanings, women entrepreneurs are connected with champions to enhance their business skills. Some Gender Working Group members are among PUE entrepreneurs (see example above). Gender Working Group members share their experiences during monthly meetings, demonstrating various income-generating activities made possible through energy access. As a result, three savings groups have been established by the members.
